docs.summary: Sends async continuations back to the main thread, so `await` in game code resumes where the scene actually lives.
docs.remarks:
Without a synchronization context everything after an `await` resumes on a thread pool thread, and ordinary game code ends up touching the scene from the wrong thread, which only sometimes crashes. Installing one makes await behave the way the code reads.

Each context is one session. The editor ends a session when play starts or stops and when scripts reload: the session token is cancelled and every continuation still waiting on it is dropped, so a method that awaited during play never resumes against the edit scene or runs code that was reloaded. A dropped method simply stops, so its `finally` blocks do not run. Work that must clean up watches [`SessionToken`](#api~Prowl.Runtime.Tasks.MainThreadContext~SessionToken) instead.

Gameplay work stays tied to its session across threads: anything started from a scene callback or from main thread queued work carries the session with its execution context, so a worker that hops back with `await GameTask.MainThread()` after its session ended is dropped too. Everything else, such as editor code, long lived threads and work that suppresses execution context flow, follows the current session. Blocking [`Send`](#api~Prowl.Runtime.Tasks.MainThreadContext~Send) calls are the exception and carry over, since a thread is waiting on them.

docs.summary: The context the engine installed, or null when no loop is running.

The session the calling code belongs to: the current one on the main thread, and on a worker the one that started the gameplay work it is running, falling back to the current one. After [`Stop`](#api~Prowl.Runtime.Tasks.MainThreadContext~Stop) it is the stopped session, so anything asking for the main thread is refused. Null when no loop is running.
Whether the caller is on the thread the engine pumps.

Whether the caller is on the engine's thread, for main thread only APIs to check themselves. True when no context has been installed (tests, tools, early startup), since there is no engine thread to be off yet and refusing to run would be worse than the race being guarded against.
How much work is waiting for the next pump.
Completes at the start of the next [`Pump`](#api~Prowl.Runtime.Tasks.MainThreadContext~Pump), or is cancelled if the session ends first.

docs.summary: Completes at the start of the first [`Pump`](#api~Prowl.Runtime.Tasks.MainThreadContext~Pump) where `ready` returns true, checked on the main thread once per frame. Cancelled if the session ends first, so it never hangs.
Installs a context bound to the calling thread, which must be the one running the loop. Replaces any installed one the way [`Restart`](#api~Prowl.Runtime.Tasks.MainThreadContext~Restart) does.

Ends the current session and starts a new one on the same thread. Must be called on the main thread. Called from inside async code, the thread's synchronization context is put back by the runtime when that code returns, so the next [`Pump`](#api~Prowl.Runtime.Tasks.MainThreadContext~Pump) points it at the new session again.

Ends the session for good, for when the loop stops. Blocked [`Send`](#api~Prowl.Runtime.Tasks.MainThreadContext~Send) calls still queued run here. Until [`Uninstall`](#api~Prowl.Runtime.Tasks.MainThreadContext~Uninstall) the ownership checks stay armed and any request for the main thread is refused, so a worker cannot run main thread work alongside the shutdown.
Stops the loop if it is still running and removes it, so every thread counts as the main thread again.

docs.summary: Runs everything queued for the main thread. Called once per frame by the game loop.
docs.remarks: Drains a snapshot of what was already waiting rather than looping until empty, so a continuation that queues more work cannot keep the pump running and stall the frame.
